question: A legal-document analysis agent has a single retrieve_clause tool that can pull arbitrary text ranges from any uploaded file by byte offset, which the model frequently misuses to grab unrelated or malformed spans. The team wants to replace it with a constrained alternative that only ever returns whole, well-defined clauses. Which redesign best follows the pattern of replacing a generic tool with a constrained one?
options: A) Keep retrieve_clause unchanged and add a second agent whose only job is to double-check the byte ranges after retrieval
B) Replace retrieve_clause with a get_clause_by_id tool that only accepts a validated clause identifier from a pre-parsed clause index
C) Keep retrieve_clause but double the number of example byte-offset calls in its description so the model learns better offsets
D) Give the agent broader access by also adding a raw_file_read tool so it can cross-check offsets against the full document
correct_answers: B) Replace retrieve_clause with a get_clause_by_id tool that only accepts a validated clause identifier from a pre-parsed clause index
explanations: Incorrect. Adding a checking agent works around the problem after the fact rather than constraining the tool itself, and increases pipeline complexity without fixing the root cause.

Correct. Swapping the unconstrained byte-offset tool for get_clause_by_id, which only accepts validated identifiers from a pre-parsed index, mirrors the documented pattern of replacing a generic tool with a narrower one that structurally prevents the misuse.
Incorrect. More examples may improve offset guesses somewhat, but the tool still accepts arbitrary byte ranges, so the structural cause of malformed spans remains unaddressed.
Incorrect. Adding another broad, unconstrained tool increases the surface for misuse and decision complexity rather than replacing the problematic tool with a scoped alternative.
